angle: This is a control deck that happens to own eleven infinite lines — the engine assembles itself in roughly three games out of four while every named kill needs a wish, so the issue teaches you to pilot the draw engine and hold the four ceilings until the arithmetic says go.

teases: MIRKWOOD BATS: 13 DRAINS ON ONE ENGINE, 2 ON THE OTHER — AND ON THE SECOND IT SWITCHES THE ENGINE OFF
BLOOD ARTIST REFUTED AS A KILL: 8 LIFE TOTAL, A 3.5x PENALTY FOR ONE WORD OF TEMPLATING
THE ENGINE NEEDS NO TUTOR — 73 TO 74% BY TURN TEN WITH NO WISHES SPENT
FOUR NAMED KILLS, ONE OF THEM VERIFIED — AND THE HONEST NUMBER IS A UNION NOBODY MEASURED

departments.headline: DRAW FIRST. DRAIN SECOND.
departments.dek: Why does a deck holding eleven infinite lines want you spending turn four drawing cards? Because the engine turns up on its own in three games out of four, and the kills only turn up when you go and fetch them.

callouts.title: BUY A BODY
callouts.text: Renewable fodder is the class the sim finds earliest — mean turn 2.796, and you have it by turn ten in 73.6% of games with no tutor involved. Bitterblossom, Reassembling Skeleton and Gravecrawler are the three you most want to see.

callouts.title: OPEN THE VALVE
callouts.text: A free sacrifice outlet arrives at mean turn 2.803 and sits at 73.8% by turn ten unassisted. Carrion Feeder and Viscera Seer cost one mana and never ask for another one.

callouts.title: LAND THE PHYSICIAN
callouts.text: The commander hits the battlefield on turn four in 7,249 games out of 10,000, mean 4.283, and he is down by turn six in 91.7%. From that turn on, every spare creature is a card.

callouts.title: HOLD THE PAYOFF
callouts.text: You have a drain by turn ten in 66.9% of games unassisted. Keep it in hand until the turn it converts — a deployed drain is a target and an undeployed one is a surprise.

captions.Yawgmoth, Thran Physician: **THE ENGINE:** no mana anywhere in the cost, so no tax and no Winter Orb effect ever touches it — the price is one life and one spare body, at instant speed, on anybody's turn.
captions.Bitterblossom: **THE BEST TURN TWO IN THE DECK:** a Faerie every upkeep for 1 life and no card spent, and it rebuilds through a sweeper by itself.
captions.Nest of Scarabs: **THE HUB:** it hands back one body for the counter each activation spends — one only, and only after the death, so the chain is body-neutral just while the counter lands on something that lives.

pilot_tips.text: Activate him on the end step before your untap — the ability costs no mana, so holding it up all round costs you nothing.
Keep two mana open on an empty board; the Skeleton alone makes it an engine turn.

departments.pull_quote: Three games in four hand you the engine off the top of your library. Pace for that game — it is the median one.

departments.headline: CAN IT MAKE A BODY AND KILL IT?
departments.dek: The keep test is not whether you have the kill, because on seven cards you almost never do. It is whether the hand makes bodies and can spend one for free.

hands.why: Three lands is the modal kept hand — 3,586 of the sim's keeps hold exactly three. Fodder, a free outlet, an ignition source and a drain are the four classes the model finds earliest at mean turns 2.796, 2.803, 2.868 and 3.014, and this hand already holds all four.

Fast mana with a black source is a hand ahead of the curve it was dealt. It is the thinnest class on the sheet at 43.5% unassisted by turn ten, and 707 games out of 10,000 cast the commander on turn two — every one of them started here.

Payoffs with nothing underneath them are blanks until something is dying, and enablers at least dig toward a payoff. Then price the top end: {3}{B}{B}{B} against 3.910 mean available mana on turn four is a turn-seven card, not a keep.

The dream pair with nothing under it. Stack 001 proved that loop unbounded and then named its price — the drain plus two other creatures on the battlefield when it starts. The rest of this hand costs four and six.

captions.Dark Ritual: **THE TURN-TWO HAND:** one black into three, which is the whole early-commander plan in a single card. Fast mana is 43.5% unassisted, so a hand already holding it is ahead of a curve most of your games never get.
captions.Skullclamp: **KEEPABLE ON ITS OWN:** one mana, and every 1/1 the deck manufactures becomes two cards. It is the draw engine that still works on the turns the commander is answered.

pilot_tips.text: Never mulligan a hand for lacking the commander — he is in the command zone, not in your library.

departments.pull_quote: Two to five lands is your band. The sim keeps its first seven 82.3% of the time at a mean of 0.209 mulligans — you get to be picky, and you almost never have to be.

departments.headline: THREE PAYOFFS, FIVE OPEN LANDS
departments.dek: Grave Pact is on the battlefield, three payoffs are in your hand, and the Azorius seat has held five untapped lands through two rotations. Pick one before you read a word of the Coach's answer.
departments.pull_quote: You cannot kill anybody this turn. So stop asking which payoff is biggest and start asking which one is still there next turn.
departments.note: Renderer: the issue's only decision spread. Branch cards must stay ahead of the recommendation — the reader commits before the Coach shows his hand (STYLEv3 §5.1). The pull quote is deliberately non-telegraphing because dept_furniture prints above the spread.

departments.headline: THE QUIET SEAT NOBODY BELIEVES
departments.dek: You arrive on the table's radar at turn four, because that is when your best card lands. So what do three opponents actually read off your board — and how do you spend that reading instead of resenting it?

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW: THE BATS BOARD
callouts.text: Mirkwood Bats beside Yawgmoth and Nest of Scarabs is thirteen triggers — 13 from every seat, 52 across a four-opponent pod, verified five separate ways. Present that board on a turn you can act, never a turn earlier.

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW: THE BLOWFLY BOARD
callouts.text: Blowfly Infestation beside Nest of Scarabs, with a death-metering drain and two spare bodies already down, is the real thing: 38 completed iterations take four opponents from 40 to 0.

callouts.title: THE TELL YOU CANNOT HIDE
callouts.text: Mikaeus is the shared half of seven of the eleven two-card infinites on the bracket sheet. The table's cheapest correct answer to your whole deck is one exile effect pointed at one creature. Do not teach them that.

callouts.title: LEAD FODDER, HOLD THE HUB
callouts.text: Cast Nest of Scarabs on the turn it pays, not the turn you can first afford it. With a three-card assembly, the last piece down is the one everybody would have answered.

captions.Grave Pact: **THE ROOM-CHANGER:** a drain takes life quietly and privately; an edict takes a creature from three players in front of everybody, every turn, forever.
captions.Exquisite Blood: **THE ONE NOBODY SEES COMING:** it does nothing visible on the turn it lands. Deploy South Wind Avatar first — a 3/4 deathtouch body reads as fair.
captions.Necropotence: **WHAT ACTUALLY DRAINS YOU:** the engine is roughly life-neutral once a drain is out. This, Bitterblossom and Black Market Connections are the cards taking your life total down.

pilot_tips.text: Fire it on the end step before your untap — the table watches a card leave your hand for a reason they cannot name until it is too late.

departments.pull_quote: A scary board is a clock and the table will price it as a kill. That is a sequencing problem, which is the good kind — you solve those for free.

departments.headline: WHO WANTS YOU DEAD
departments.dek: Assign your role at the start of every game and re-ask it after every board change. Against a fair pod you own the long game — and against exactly one archetype you are the beatdown, while staying the control against everyone else at the same table.

threats.read: Your best matchup, and you are allowed to look cheerful about it. Two decks both claiming inevitability means the cheaper rebuild wins, and yours is structural rather than held: Reassembling Skeleton returns for {1}{B} forever with no board condition, Gravecrawler recasts for {B} while a Zombie is out, and Bitterblossom and Black Market Connections make a body a turn without spending a card. Deploy the fodder freely and keep the drain in hand until the turn it converts. The one board that genuinely costs you is enchantment removal on Nest of Scarabs, because nothing in the 99 rebuys an enchantment — that is the case where your tutor is a rebuild rather than a finish, and you spend it that way without flinching.

Split this one in half before you panic. Pay 1 life, sacrifice another creature — that costs no mana, so a Sphere effect never touches the engine once the commander has resolved. Deployment is the vulnerable window, not operation. Two real exposures remain: fast mana is three cards at 43.5% unassisted, so a tax landing before turn four genuinely delays a commander whose mean cast turn is 4.283; and a resolved Cursed Totem or a Pithing Needle switches off every creature outlet at once. Your outlets underneath those are the ones that are not creatures, and the Blowfly loop is triggered rather than activated, so it runs under both.

You are the aggressor's target and the pod's stabiliser at once, and this deck is unusually good at holding both jobs. Grave Pact is the card that does it — every creature you sacrifice edicts every other player, so an aggressive board is dismantled by an engine you were running anyway. Answer boards, not threats: four sweepers plus nine debuff effects is the breadth you lack everywhere else, while three dedicated instants means the bar for spot removal is 'ends the game or ends my deck's function'. And stop spending life one turn early — the commander's cost, Warren Soultrader's cost, Bitterblossom and Black Market Connections all draw from the pool the aggro deck is attacking.

The unfavourable one, and against that seat you are the beatdown while remaining the control against everyone else. Your interaction on a combo turn is three instants, two of which only answer creatures, and there are no counterspells to go and find. That is what the engine costs and it is a fair price you pay with speed. So hold nothing: against combo, the last profitable moment for an answer is now. Then be the faster clock with a floor — the four enabler classes sit at 73 to 74% unassisted and around 90% tutor-assisted by turn ten, and one Mirkwood Bats assembly removes 52 of the pod's 160 life. Pace for the engine, not for the tutored kill.

This one earns its own box because it costs you quality rather than function. Gravecrawler, Reassembling Skeleton, Persist, Victimize, Animate Dead and Phyrexian Reclamation all read from the graveyard, so a Rest in Peace effect converts renewable fodder back into one-shot fodder — precisely the axis your consistency is bought on. Know which half goes quiet, because it is not the half people assume: dies means is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, so under a graveyard replacement your death-metered payoffs stop, and Grave Pact stops with them. Your creation-side payoffs keep paying. That is a read from oracle text rather than a checked line, and it tells you which drain to fetch.

captions.Plumb the Forbidden: **THE WRATH, CONVERTED:** sacrifice any number of creatures in response and the spell copies itself once each — their sweeper announcement becomes your draw step.
captions.Bojuka Bog: **A FREE ANSWER IN A LAND SLOT:** it enters tapped, so bank it for the turn their graveyard matters instead of spending it on curve.

pilot_tips.text: Do not wait for Nest of Scarabs to pay you off this one — minus X/minus X is not counters, so the hub stays silent.

departments.pull_quote: Held answers rot. Against combo, or against lethal already on the board, the last profitable moment is now.

departments.headline: DON'T TUTOR FOR THE ENGINE
departments.dek: Five wishes, and the first thing to understand is what they are not for. This engine finds itself in roughly three games out of four. So what do you actually go and get — and why does the answer change with which loop is already on the battlefield?

callouts.title: NEVER WISH FOR A CLASS YOU ALREADY GET
callouts.text: Renewable fodder, a free outlet and an ignition source each sit at 73 to 74% unassisted by turn ten. A tutor lifts them to roughly 90% — a seventeen-point gain on a class the deck was handing you anyway.

callouts.title: FETCH THE RIGHT DRAIN
callouts.text: On the verified board, Bastion of Remembrance removes 7 life from each opponent, 28 across a four-opponent pod. Zulaport Cutthroat does the same 7 and 28 by a different route. Blood Artist in the same slot removes eight life in total. Target player against each opponent is a factor of 3.5.

callouts.title: FETCH FOR THE ENGINE YOU ARE ON
callouts.text: Mirkwood Bats is thirteen triggers on the Yawgmoth line and two on the Blowfly line, where it also halts the loop outright. Which engine is on the battlefield decides whether it is the best drain in your library or the worst.

callouts.title: COUNT BODIES BEFORE YOU WISH
callouts.text: The Blowfly loop needs the drain plus two other creatures already on the battlefield when it starts. Short one body, your wish is a three-mana enchantment that does nothing.

captions.Beseech the Mirror: **THE WISH THAT CASTS:** bargained, it plays what it finds for free at mana value 4 or less — which reaches Nest of Scarabs, Mirkwood Bats and Grave Pact, and does not reach Exquisite Blood at five.
captions.Diabolic Intent: **THE COST THAT ISN'T:** the creature you sacrifice is a death trigger here, so the best tutoring rate in the deck is the one everybody else files as a drawback.
captions.Demonic Tutor: **NO CONDITIONS, NO CEILING:** the only wish that does not care what the card costs — and one of the four Game Changers driving the bracket floor.

pilot_tips.text: Cast both Spree modes in one go and point the draw at yourself — you book the card and draw it on the same turn.

departments.pull_quote: You are not tutoring to make this deck function. You are tutoring to convert.

departments.headline: THE CARD YOU NEVER HAVE TO DRAW
departments.dek: One card in this deck is exempt from variance and the rules say so in a single sentence. What is that guarantee worth to a mono-black engine — and what does the second trip actually cost?
departments.body:
Begin with the clause that makes this format unlike every other one. CR 903.8: "A player may cast a commander they own from the command zone." Yawgmoth is therefore not a card you draw. He is a card you have. The simulation puts him on the battlefield in 9,847 of 10,000 games, mean turn 4.283, and 7,249 of those cast him on turn four exactly.

The exhibit beside it is the price of the guarantee, and it compounds. The same rule adds "an additional {2} for each previous time the player casting it has cast it from the command zone that game." Four mana, then six, then eight, then ten. Set that schedule against mean available mana of 3.910 on turn four and 7.103 on turn ten. The plain-English holding is short. The first recast costs you a turn. The second costs you the whole turn. The third is a turn nobody is going to give you.

Colour identity is CR 903.4, and it is the constraint that built the other ninety-eight cards. One black symbol in the cost, one colour in the deck — and the audit comes back clean: black is 100% of the pip load and 100% of the sources, on curve at 96.0% once ramp is counted. What it costs is breadth. This library holds no counterspell, no artifact removal and no enchantment removal, and none of the five tutors can find one, because there is none to find. That is the format's bargain stated as a rule rather than as a complaint.

Commander damage next, because the record disposes of it quickly. CR 903.10a removes a player who has been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander. Yawgmoth is a 2/4 who would very much rather be sacrificing than attacking, and twenty-one damage is eleven connections. Commander damage is a coincidence in this deck, not a clock.

Now the clause to memorise, because it cuts in both directions. CR 702.16b: "A permanent or player with protection can't be targeted by spells with the stated quality and can't be targeted by abilities from a source with the stated quality." Yawgmoth has protection from Humans and is himself a Human Cleric, so his own ability can never target him. Read that twice — it is the exact clause that bounds every engine in The Kill, because the 2/4 who could comfortably absorb four counters is not allowed to take one. In the other direction it is free armour in a format thick with Human commanders, and CR 702.16f keeps Human creatures from blocking him besides.

One last fact about the zone before the corner office speaks. Three opponents can see it. They cannot see your hand. What they price when this commander resolves is a reputation rather than a board — and the bracket sheet agrees with them, landing at floor 4 on four Game Changers and eleven two-card infinites.

COACH'S READ. One decision, and you make it early: buy the insurance before the removal, never after. Lightning Greaves equips at sorcery speed only, so the turn to arm him is the turn before you need him. Malakir Rebirth and Supernatural Stamina both return him to the battlefield rather than to the zone, which means the tax never advances at all — they are the cheapest recasts in the deck precisely because they are not recasts. And price the second trip before you make the first: six mana spent getting him back is six mana not spent on the hub. Then remember what he is for. Use him as a draw engine for three or four turns before you ever use him as a kill.

captions.Lightning Greaves: **INSURANCE, NOT ARMOUR:** it equips at sorcery speed only, so the turn to arm him is the turn before you need it — and the shroud cuts you off from your own tricks too.

pilot_tips.text: Return him to the battlefield rather than to the command zone — a rescue is not a recast, so the tax never advances.

departments.headline: WHAT EVERY SEAT IS FOR
departments.dek: Ten groups, and the order is the order they matter in. Read the first three and you know how this deck works; read the rest and you know why it keeps working after somebody answers one of them.

roster.role: The payoffs — creation side and death side
Interaction — all of it aimed at creatures
The mana — 36 copies, 35 of them black

callouts.title: THE HUB HAS NO SPARE
callouts.text: Nest of Scarabs is a singleton enchantment, and nothing in the 99 rebuys an enchantment — Persist, Victimize, Animate Dead, Phyrexian Reclamation and Agadeem's Awakening all read creature card. That is the one removal spell that costs you a tutor.

callouts.title: CREATION SIDE VERSUS DEATH SIDE
callouts.text: Bastion of Remembrance, Zulaport Cutthroat, Blood Artist and South Wind Avatar all meter deaths. Mirkwood Bats and Ayara get paid when a body arrives. On the same board that is thirteen triggers against seven, and it is the widest measured gap the deck owns.

callouts.title: WHERE THE GRAPH IS BLIND
callouts.text: Seven cards in this 99 have no entry in the retrieval graph at all, and one of them is Nest of Scarabs. Thirty-nine synergy edges fall inside the deck. A shortlist selected over every tagged card in the format cannot tell you how well a card fits this list, and it does not pretend to.

captions.Ayara, First of Locthwain: **PAID ON ARRIVAL:** Nest of Scarabs makes black Insects and Ayara reads 'another black creature you control enters', so she collects where the death-metered drains starve. Her tap ability is a second free outlet that draws.
captions.Warren Soultrader: **THREE JOBS, ONE SLOT:** a free repeatable outlet, a Treasure per body, and a Zombie that switches Gravecrawler on. Its cost is 1 life — the same currency the commander spends.
captions.Massacre Girl, Known Killer: **WITHER AS A BUSINESS MODEL:** your combat damage arrives as -1/-1 counters, and every one of them is a Nest trigger. The draw clause only reads opponents' creatures, so point it outward.

pilot_tips.text: Size X for the board you want gone and treat the Insects as upside — the token count from one multi-creature X has not been settled.

departments.pull_quote: Forty-two contained lines over about twenty pieces. Answer one kill and you have rarely answered only one.

departments.headline: BUY THE MANA, THEN BUY THE BRANCH
departments.dek: Ten cards, ranked, and not one of them names Mikaeus. Two are free stock sitting in another box; the rest are the cheapest way to stop seven of your eleven infinites resting on a single body.

callouts.title: WHY THE LIST ROUTES AROUND ONE CARD
callouts.text: Mikaeus carries seven of eleven two-card infinites, so the answer is not to buy more cards that need him. Plague Belcher, Walking Ballista and Triskelion all top the combo-opener list and none of them is here. Pawn of Ulamog completes seven lines that never name him; Drivnod completes five.

callouts.title: AN INDEX CANNOT SEE A CREATURE TYPE
callouts.text: The first fodder recommendation off the machine was Ophiomancer, whose token only arrives if you control no Snakes — and South Wind Avatar is the only Snake in the 100. It would go blank on exactly the board you most want. Bontu's Monument took the slot instead, and nothing in the 99 can switch it off.

callouts.title: THE OBSOLESCENCE INDEX IS WRONG ABOUT TWO CARDS
callouts.text: It lists a strictly-better replacement for both Ayara and Mirkwood Bats. Reading the cards refutes it here: that replacement's drain is single-target, and a single-target drain was measured at a 3.5x penalty against the each-opponent class. The index is format-agnostic and does not know which side of the trigger this deck is paid on.

callouts.title: NOT ONE LINE ON THIS LIST IS VERIFIED
callouts.text: Every combo a pick would open is recorded, contained and unresolved. They stay candidates until a stack passes — which is exactly the standing this magazine gives them.

captions.Cabal Coffers: **FIRST BUY:** 22 Swamps means Coffers taps for more black than the rest of the mana base by turn five, and it costs a land slot rather than a spell slot.
captions.Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth: **THE MULTIPLIER:** on its own in mono-black it is a Swamp with legend rules attached. Beside Coffers or Crypt Ghast it turns every land in the deck into one.

departments.pull_quote: What raises this deck's power is verification, not addition. A twelfth two-card infinite moves nothing — the floor is already there.

departments.headline: ONE COLOUR, ONE QUESTION
departments.dek: Mono-black makes half of this audit trivial — pip share and source share cannot disagree when there is only one colour to be short of. So the only question left is how many, and the yardstick answers it with a caveat worth reading twice.

callouts.title: THE HALF-POINT SHORTFALL
callouts.text: The audit wants 36 black sources for a 90% on-curve rate. Thirty-five of the deck's 36 land copies make black — Ancient Tomb is the one that does not — so lands alone land at 89.5%. That gap is arithmetic, not a build error, and in a 36-land deck the target is a yardstick rather than a possibility.

callouts.title: TEN NONLAND PRODUCERS CLOSE IT
callouts.text: Four rocks, four rituals and two dorks lift the count to 43 sources and on-curve black to 96.0%. Read what each class buys: the rituals are early-commander mana, and the dorks are engine mana, which is a different resource — they turn a creature dying into castable black.

callouts.title: THREE PRODUCERS THAT SCORE ZERO
callouts.text: Sol Ring, Ancient Tomb and Ashnod's Altar make nothing coloured under the unconditional-mana rule. They buy speed, never fixing. Restricted mana anywhere in the 99: none.

callouts.title: FOUR ENTER TAPPED, AND IT MATTERS HERE
callouts.text: Archway Commons, Bojuka Bog, Castle Locthwain and Path of Ancestry are the whole tapped list. That is about as low a tap rate as a mana base gets, and it counts double for a deck whose commander activates at instant speed for no mana. An untapped land is an activation you can hold up.

captions.Swamp: **TWENTY-TWO OF THEM:** the untapped backbone, and the reason Snuff Out costs four life instead of four mana. In mono-black the basic is the best land in the deck.
captions.Phyrexian Tower: **A LAND THAT SACRIFICES:** a free outlet that makes {B}{B} while it does it. Where a spare body is a resource, this is one of the best untapped lands you can draw.

departments.pull_quote: Seventy-five black pips across 54 cards, up to triple-black in one cost — and the first pip is demanded on turn one.

departments.headline: THE ENGINE SHOWS UP. THE KILL GETS FETCHED.
departments.dek: Ten thousand simulated openings, one fixed seed, no interaction and no opponents. What they measure is which half of this deck you can count on — and the gap between the two columns is the deck's whole personality.

callouts.title: READ EVERY FIGURE AS A PAIR
callouts.text: The first number excludes tutors, rituals and cost reducers entirely; the second lets one drawn, affordable tutor fill one missing half. Renewable fodder 73.6% / 90.3%. A free outlet 73.8% / 90.0%. An ignition source 73.0% / 90.2%. A drain 66.9% / 87.7%. Engine mana 60.6% / 85.0%.

callouts.title: FOUR KILLS, NOT ONE
callouts.text: Tutor-assisted by turn ten: Blowfly Infestation plus Nest of Scarabs 32.1%, the Mikaeus package 26.2%, Exquisite Blood plus South Wind Avatar 32.5%, Warren Soultrader plus Gravecrawler plus a drain 20.0%. Unassisted they are 2.6%, 1.7%, 2.9% and 1.1% — which is what a tutor is really buying.

callouts.title: THE NUMBER WE REFUSE TO PRINT
callouts.text: Those four lines are independent and overlapping, so the honest quantity is their union — and nothing computes one, because the target schema is an AND of ORs and cannot express a union. It is unmeasured and strictly greater than 32.5%. The sheet's one composite row spans two of the four; it is not this deck's kill rate and we will not quote it as one.

callouts.title: THE COMMANDER'S HISTOGRAM
callouts.text: Turn four in 7,249 games out of 10,000, mean 4.283, median 4, on the battlefield by turn six in 91.7%. Turn two happens 707 times, and every one of those games opened with fast mana.

callouts.title: WHAT THE SIM IS NOT
callouts.text: It models resource development, not games — no interaction, no removal, no politics, and a target counts as assembled when the cards are drawn. Read it as a floor on what turns up, never as a prediction of what happens.

departments.pull_quote: Three quarters unassisted for the engine. A fifth to a third, with a wish spent, for any one kill.

departments.headline: EIGHT LINES, ARGUED AND AFFIRMED
departments.dek: Eight scenarios went to the checker and eight came back signed. Three of them say a famous line does not do what the database promised — and those three are the most useful pages in this issue.

callouts.title: THE LOOP THAT RUNS FOREVER, AND PAYS THREE
callouts.text: Blowfly Infestation plus Nest of Scarabs is genuinely unbounded — the counter is still on the Insect when it dies, so the intervening 'if' is satisfied every time. On a thin board it is also nearly drainless: the drain is the only creature left, Blowfly is mandatory and needs a target, so it eats your payoff on iteration one for a total of 3 per opponent. Give it the drain plus two other bodies and 38 completed iterations take four opponents from 40 to 0. Stack 001.

callouts.title: WHAT BOUNDS THE ENGINE IS BODIES
callouts.text: Protection from Humans makes a 2/4 Human Cleric untargetable by his own ability, so every counter has to land somewhere else — and once the opponent's creature is gone, that is your own tokens. Five completed activations, seven of your creatures dead, seven Bastion of Remembrance triggers, 28 life off a four-opponent pod, and your own total goes up. Spend the proliferate and it is eight and 32, a property of the line rather than the board. The two figures are never blended. Stack 002.

callouts.title: THE DRAIN THAT MUST EVENTUALLY DIE
callouts.text: Zulaport Cutthroat is a creature, so it is both a legal target and a legal sacrifice — and you are never forced to spend it, because the sacrifice is chosen when the cost is paid and 'up to one target creature' permits zero targets. Keep it through four activations, then feed it deliberately and its own leaves-the-battlefield trigger banks the seventh drain. Seven and 28 again, by a completely different route — a coincidence of arithmetic, not corroboration. Stack 003.

callouts.title: ONE WORD, A FACTOR OF 3.5
callouts.text: Blood Artist reads 'target player loses 1 life', and at a four-player table that is one seat per trigger where the others charge all of them. Eight creature deaths, eight triggers, eight life, and an exhaustive search of the line space finds nothing better. Refuted as a kill, and not narrowly: 8 against the 28 the same board produces with an each-opponent drain. Play it as reach and insurance, never as the finish. Stack 004.

callouts.title: GAINING NOTHING IS NOT GAINING
callouts.text: The sharpest edge in the deck. An Insect you sacrifice dies at toughness 1, so South Wind Avatar gains 1 and drains the table. An Insect killed by its own -1/-1 counter dies at toughness 0 — you gain 0, and gaining 0 is not a life gain event, so nothing drains. Eight death triggers, seven nonzero gains, seven drains, 28 opposing life. The Avatar's 4 toughness is worth exactly plus four activations. The database tags this pairing 'Near-infinite'; on this board that tag is wrong. Stack 005.

callouts.title: ENTERING COUNTS AS PUTTING
callouts.text: A creature that enters the battlefield already wearing a -1/-1 counter does trigger Nest of Scarabs, and the rule that decides it is the one about counters given as an object enters — not the rule the other lines lean on. So Persist is a Nest trigger as well as a reanimation, and Fume Spitter comes back as a 0/0 and dies immediately without the trigger caring. Stack 006.

callouts.title: THE BAT THAT BROKE THE LOOP
callouts.text: Mirkwood Bats on the Blowfly line triggers exactly twice, both times on the creation half, for 2 life from each opponent — worse than a death-metering drain by one. Nothing on that line is sacrificed; the Insects go to the graveyard as state-based actions for having 0 toughness, which is the game moving a permanent rather than you sacrificing one. Then the finding that should reorganise how you sequence: Bats is a 2/3, so when Blowfly is forced to target it, it survives at 1/2. Nothing dies. An unbounded engine simply switches off. Stack 007.

callouts.title: THE BAT THAT PAID TWICE
callouts.text: Activating the commander puts the ability on the stack first; the cost is paid last. So sacrificing an Insect triggers Bats while the ability is already the topmost object, that trigger goes on above it and resolves first, and the Nest token does not arrive until two resolutions later. One activation, two drains. Thirteen triggers, 13 per opponent, 52 life off a four-player table against the like-for-like 7 and 28. Thirteen is a ceiling proved five separate ways, and the last check solved the line varying only the Bat's toughness: 8, 10, 13 and 15 triggers at zero, one, two and three counter slots. Stack 008.

captions.Mirkwood Bats: **SAME CARD, OPPOSITE VERDICTS:** thirteen triggers on the commander's line, two on the Blowfly line — and on the second it switches the engine off, because its 2/3 body survives the forced counter.
captions.Blood Artist: **REFUTED, NOT DEMOTED:** eight life in total against the 28 an each-opponent drain removes from the identical board. One word of templating, a factor of 3.5.
captions.South Wind Avatar: **FOUR TOUGHNESS, FOUR ACTIVATIONS:** the sink is worth exactly plus four — and a token killed by its own counter dies at toughness 0, gains you nothing, and drains nobody.

pilot_tips.text: Feed it last, on purpose — 'up to one target creature' lets you choose zero targets, so nothing can force your drain into the engine early.

departments.pull_quote: Surviving the forced counter is fatal to a loop that needs something to die, and free money on a line that sacrifices deliberately.

departments.headline: READ IT TWICE, THEN READ THE QUOTES
departments.dek: Eight files, every citation verbatim, the checker's verdict and iteration count printed as case status. This is the section that makes the rest of the issue worth believing.
departments.pull_quote: Where the record is silent, the record is silent. Three of these eight files say a famous line does not work.

departments.headline: SEVENTY-THREE HANDS, NO HEADLINER
departments.dek: There is no standout in this deck and we are not going to invent one. The deepest credit here is two cards and twelve artists are tied at exactly that — so the feature goes to the hand that painted the face of the issue.

featured.note:
Start with the number that decides this section. Eighty-five cards counted, seventy-three different signatures, and the deepest single credit is two cards — twelve artists are tied there. Nobody dominates this deck, so nobody is going to be told they did.

Mark Winters' Yawgmoth is the Dominaria Remastered printing: the physician mid-experiment, lit from below, more surgeon than devil. It is the right read of a card whose rules text is a laboratory. Pay a life, spend a body, learn something.

One figure needs saying out loud because it is the one that lies. Jorge Jacinto's Swamp appears twenty-two times in this deck and counts once. Authorship is per card, never per copy — count it the other way and a basic land wins this section every single issue.

The printings cluster where recent Commander product does: fifteen cards from Lorwyn Eclipsed Commander, eight from Secrets of Strixhaven Commander, seven from Tarkir: Dragonstorm Commander, six from Commander Masters. Nobody curated that, and the analysis is specific about it — there is no contiguous collector-number run anywhere in the deck. This is not a drop bought whole. It is simply where the cardboard comes from, and it is most of why no single hand gets ahead.

And nothing here is foil and nothing is borderless. Eighty-two black borders and three white ones left over from Fifth and Sixth Edition. This is a working deck, sleeved at working prices, and it looks like one on purpose.

also_worth_noting.note: Animate Dead and Ashnod's Altar — two of the three white-bordered cards in the box, and both still do exactly what they did when they were printed.
Grave Pact and Massacre Girl, Known Killer: the edict and the wither engine, one hand. Both of them make somebody else's board smaller.
Crypt Ghast and Mikaeus, the Unhallowed — the same appetite twice, once starving and once very well fed.
Butcher Ghoul and Supernatural Stamina: a body that refuses to stay dead, and the trick that makes another one refuse.
Beseech the Mirror and Exquisite Blood — the wish, and the thing worth wishing for.
Black Sun's Zenith and Skullclamp: a sweeper that pays you and an equipment that kills your own tokens for cards. Two advantages wearing a disadvantage's clothes.

departments.note: Renderer: NEXT ISSUE reads 'TO BE ANNOUNCED' from issue.json — print it as authored rather than inventing a deck. Colophon carries the rules version, the decklist sha and the generation provenance.

rhythm_notes: The arc peaks twice, as designed. The Game Plan opens high and narrative; Keep or Ship steps down into practice; What's Your Play? takes it back to high participation — and this issue is the first with a real decision spread, so Act I actually delivers the participation beat instead of a [TODO]. Act II runs medium the whole way (reflection, reference, instruction) on purpose: it is the long browsing stretch between the two peaks. Act III steps down further — instruction, then browsing in The 99, then imagination in The Short List — which is the lowest point of the book and the right place for it, immediately before the density arrives. Act IV is the only dense adjacency in the issue: Sources Say (analysis) into By the Numbers (analysis), and the renderer's declared full-bleed art break sits between them, which is why the pair is legal. The Kill is the late peak and reads as narrative even though it carries the most technical content — eight callout-steps, one per verified line, is the densest furniture in the issue and it is placed where the reader has the most momentum. Act V descends cleanly: Judge's Desk is opt-in deep reference, Featured Artist is the palate cleanser, and the Back Page closes. Two deliberate breathers beyond the declared one: The Short List before Sources Say, and Featured Artist between the case files and the door out.

L10 CONFLICT, DECIDED AND FLAGGED: the brief supplies before/after deltas (combos 20 to 42, infinites 8 to 11, drains 6 to 9, fast mana 61.8% to 43.5%, fodder 78.6% to 73.6%) and a list of cards that left the deck. None of that appears anywhere in this plan, because L10 forbids describing a list the reader never saw and the validator lints for it. The current-state halves of those facts are printed instead — 42 contained lines, 11 two-card infinites, nine drains, fast mana 43.5% / 78.2%, fodder 73.6% / 90.3% — and the ten cards the pilot added are carried as ordinary members of the 99 (Gravecrawler and Reassembling Skeleton lead the fodder group, Grave Pact and Ayara are load-bearing in Table Manners and The 99, Warren Soultrader takes a caption, Exquisite Blood and Gray Merchant sit in the payoffs group). If the orchestrator wants the swap story in print, that is a constitutional amendment, not an editing note.

TIER DISCIPLINE, ENFORCED: only ONE of the four named kills is checker-verified (Blowfly Infestation + Nest of Scarabs, stack 001, and even that is verified as unbounded-and-conditional rather than as a clean kill). The Mikaeus package, Exquisite Blood + South Wind Avatar and Warren Soultrader + Gravecrawler + a drain are ◆ measured assemblies only, and every mention of them in this plan is phrased as an assembly rate or a candidate. The Kill and Judge's Desk carry the eight verified lines and nothing else.

THE BIGGEST OPEN QUESTION IS STILL OPEN: seven of the eleven two-card infinites forcing the bracket-4 floor name Mikaeus, none is verified, and on plain oracle reading undying returns a body with a +1/+1 counter that a second sacrifice would find — so they are plausibly three-card lines routing through the commander's -1/-1. Half the bracket floor rests on unresolved lines. That is printed as a finding in Table Manners and The 99; it wants a stack scenario.

STACK SCENARIOS WORTH SPAWNING, RANKED: (1) the Mikaeus family, because it decides the bracket conversation; (2) Grave Pact under the verified engine — every engine stack measured the drain and none measured the board, and seven activations is either seven edicts per seat or fourteen; (3) Exquisite Blood + South Wind Avatar, the only bracket-3 line in the 99 and the one the goldfish already credits at 32.5%; (4) Warren Soultrader + Gravecrawler + a drain, a 20.0% kill nobody has resolved in any of its four variants; (5) Ayara's exact per-activation rate against the verified 13 and 7, on stack 003's board so the figure is comparable; (6) Black Sun's Zenith + Nest of Scarabs — how many Insects does one multi-creature X actually make?

STRATEGY DB HOLES THE ISSUE HAD TO WRITE AROUND: there is no aristocrats / outlet-fodder-payoff section anywhere in the doc, nothing on what BOUNDS an iterative engine (every stack here ended by body exhaustion), no theory of trigger SURFACE (creation-side versus death-side, which is this issue's central finding), no vocabulary for a recursive copy being worth more than a one-shot one, nothing on mana-free activated abilities as a class, and nothing on how to read several partially-overlapping win conditions as one probability. The last one is why By the Numbers has to decline to print a kill rate rather than compute one.

THIN, BUT NOT EMPTY: The Short List's ten are all unverified candidates by construction, and two of them (Urborg, Culling the Weak) are owned rather than bought — the section says so. Featured Artist has no standout at all (lead credit is two cards, twelve artists tied), so it runs as a breadth feature keyed to the commander's painter; that is the honest shape, not a gap to fill.

PUN BUDGET: four, all in furniture — 'THE BAT THAT BROKE THE LOOP' / 'THE BAT THAT PAID TWICE' as a pair, 'THE COST THAT ISN'T', and 'SEVENTY-THREE HANDS, NO HEADLINER'. No pun sits in a rules explanation or a data caption.
